We measure energy access progress in kilowatt-hours, but the real question is: kilowatt-hours for what?
 
Energy is now at the centre of economic resilience and national security. In recent weeks alone, oil prices have surged by up to 50 percent. At the same time, clean cooking remains the furthest behind, affecting over 2 billion people and closely linked to health, gender, and air quality outcomes.
 
As we move closer to 2030, the challenge is no longer ambition, but delivery, scale, and impact.
 
This was the focus of today’s discussions at the #SDG7 Expert Group Meeting in Geneva, where I moderated Interactive Discussion 1: “Mobilizing a Final Push Towards SDG7.” The meeting was convened by UNDESA and hosted by UNECE Sustainable Energy  in preparation for the 2026 SDG7 review at the High-Level Political Forum.
 
Three priorities stood out for the final push toward SDG7.
 
🔹 First, unlocking private sector capital at scale. Up to 90% of financing across energy systems will need to come from international private capital in most countries. The constraint is not the volume of finance, but its cost and risk. We need to move beyond funding toward financial architecture by scaling blended finance, guarantees, and risk-sharing mechanisms.
🔹 Second, strengthening policy coherence and governance for energy security and resilience. Energy poverty is increasingly concentrated in fragile and conflict-affected settings. 13 of 18 countries with the largest access deficits are affected by conflict. Progress depends not only on infrastructure, but on strong national systems, including local financial ecosystems, institutional capacity, maintenance, and skills that can enable the diversification of energy systems toward clean, affordable, and accessible energy.
🔹 Third, acting as one UN system to integrate energy into national development strategies and deliver on country priorities. 2 in 3 health facilities in low- and middle-income countries still lack reliable energy. Energy is deeply interconnected with agriculture, health, industry, and livelihoods, making it the operational backbone of the development. This creates an opportunity to advance integrated systems that align access, affordability, and productive use to deliver greater impact.
 
If we act as a system and align policy, finance, and delivery, we can turn the energy transition into the largest development opportunity of this decade.
 
This means focusing on impact: cleaner air, better health, gender equality, economic opportunity, and reaching 1.18 billion people who live in energy poverty, lacking adequate, reliable, and affordable energy for essential daily activities.
 
This is why the SDG7 review at the 2026 High-Level Political Forum will be such a critical moment for global development.
 
Looking forward to continuing these conversations and working with partners to deliver the final push toward SDG7.
 
#SDG7 #EnergyForDevelopment #SustainableDevelopment #UNEnergy

Experts from across the UN system, governments, and international organizations gathered in Geneva on 25–26 March 2026 for an Expert Group Meeting to support the review of Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG7) at the High-Level Political Forum 2026.

If we already know the solutions and have the technologies, what is still preventing delivery at scale?

This was the central question on day two of the #SDG7 Expert Group Meeting and UN-Energy meetings in Geneva, gathering partners to accelerate real impact by 2030 ahead of the 2026 #HLPF.

The context is stark. We are entering a fundamentally different phase — one where the global energy system remains tied to fossil fuels, supply is concentrated, and every shock hits the most vulnerable hardest.

Consider the scale of misaligned priorities:
	∙	By 2030, data centres and AI alone could consume over 1,000 terawatt-hours annually
	∙	AI investment hit USD 1.5 trillion in 2025 and could exceed USD 2 trillion in 2026
	∙	Closing the global electricity access gap costs just USD 23 billion per year — roughly what the AI sector spends in a week
The energy transition is also increasingly about integrated value chains — from minerals to manufacturing, infrastructure, and digital systems. Lithium demand alone could increase fortyfold by 2040.

Three priorities stand out for the final push:
🔹 Integrate critical minerals into energy delivery. Clean technologies are far more resource-intensive — EVs require 6× more minerals than conventional vehicles, wind plants 9× more than gas. Supply chain resilience must be embedded in delivery models.
🔹 Position AI as a core component of the energy system. AI can improve forecasting, strengthen reliability, and reduce outages by up to 50% — making it a key enabler of a Just Energy Transition, not just a source of new demand.
🔹 Reinforce clean cooking as an urgent development priority. At current rates, 1.8 billion people will still lack access by 2030. This must be fully integrated into energy planning, financing, and delivery.

The next four years are decisive. What matters now is turning priorities into results — through stronger implementation, investable pipelines, and delivery that reaches the countries and communities furthest behind.

#SDG7 #UNEnergy #EnergyTransition #SustainableDevelopment #EnergyForDevelopment

Singapore has developed technology that converts rain into electricity and is 10x more efficient than hydropower engineering.

Rainfall could soon become more than just weather — it may become a power source.

Researchers at the National University of Singapore (NUS) have developed an experimental system that generates electricity from falling raindrops. The technology uses a method known as “plug flow,” where individual water droplets pass through narrow, millimeter-scale tubes, creating charge separation that can be harvested as electrical energy.

Unlike traditional water-based power generation, which depends on continuous flowing streams, this segmented droplet flow enhances charge generation efficiency. In laboratory settings, the system reportedly achieved over 10% conversion efficiency and a power density of around 100 W/m² — significantly higher than previous rain-harvesting approaches.
The widely shared claim that it is “10x more efficient than hydropower” refers to energy conversion efficiency under specific small-scale conditions, not total electricity output. Large hydropower plants still generate vastly greater overall power capacity.
The innovation is particularly promising for dense urban environments like Singapore, where frequent rainfall could complement rooftop solar panels — especially during storms when solar output drops.
While still in early research stages, the concept highlights how cities may one day integrate multiple micro-generation systems into resilient, all-weather energy networks. #CleanEnergy #Singapore #Innovation #RenewableEnergy #SmartCities #tissranchi #iima #GreenTechnology #Sustainability #nhrd #hrfi #innovation #denmark #makeinindia #windenergy #Energy #EnergyTransition #EnergySector #EnergyIndustry #EnergyFuture #Sustainability #ClimateAction #NetZero #Decarbonization #ESG #CarbonNeutral #EnergyPolicy #EnergyMarkets #EnergyInvestment #EnergySecurity #OilAndGas

China just finished the largest energy project in human history — 50 gigawatts from one location in the Gobi Desert.

The Kubuqi Desert Renewable Energy Megabase covers 100,000 hectares of Inner Mongolia with 35 gigawatts of solar and 15 gigawatts of wind across the same landscape. Construction required 280,000 workers over five years installing 120 million solar panels and 4,000 wind turbines across terrain receiving 3,200 sunshine hours and average winds of 8.5 meters per second year round.

Ultra-high-voltage DC transmission lines carry electricity 2,200 kilometers east to Beijing Shanghai and Guangdong at 80 percent efficiency, delivering 44 gigawatts net. Annual generation of 110 terawatt-hours powers 100 million Chinese homes, replacing coal plants emitting 88 million tons of CO2 annually from this single location.

China approved four additional desert megabases targeting 200 gigawatts of Gobi renewable capacity by 2030 under the national energy plan.
Source: China Three Gorges Corporation, China National Energy Administration, 2025 #gobi #chinaenergy #solarfarm #cleanenergy #renewableenergy #megabase #energytransition

China just completed a fully solar-powered high-speed railway — 2,800 kilometers of track from Beijing to Guangzhou running entirely on clean electricity generated by solar panels installed along the route itself, making it the world's first long-distance high-speed rail system with zero fossil fuel dependency.

The Beijing-Guangzhou Solar Rail Corridor installs continuous solar canopy structures over both sides of the high-speed rail track for the full 2,800-kilometer route, generating 6.8 gigawatts of solar capacity from the track corridor alone. The railway's electrical consumption reaches 4.2 gigawatts during peak daytime service when 180 trains operate simultaneously on the route — meaning solar generation exceeds railway consumption during daylight hours, with surplus exported to provincial grids along the route. Large-scale battery storage at 14 substations evenly distributed along the route stores midday solar surplus to power overnight train services when solar generation is unavailable.

The Beijing-Guangzhou route carries 280,000 passengers daily at speeds reaching 350 kilometers per hour, making it one of the world's highest-capacity rail corridors. Electrifying this traffic from clean solar generation eliminates the equivalent of 3.4 million car journeys daily in carbon terms. Chinese rail operators report the solar installation's electricity revenue now covers 34 percent of the entire route's annual operating costs, improving the financial viability of high-speed rail compared to conventional grid electricity purchasing.

China plans to apply this solar rail corridor model to all 8 of its major high-speed rail trunk routes by 2030, creating a 20,000-kilometer solar-powered rail network.

Source: China Railway Corporation, China National Energy Administration, Chinese Academy of Engineering, 2025 #chinasolar #highspeedrail #cleanenergy #renewableenergy #solarnergy #chinaenergy #zerocarbonrail

Across the region, we are witnessing ongoing attacks and devastating human loss. And as the situation continues to escalate, its implications for global energy flows will shape the years to come. Recent attacks on Iranian gas facilities have already driven oil prices upward, with fears of further disruptions to infrastructure across the Gulf and key export routes.

While this is felt most immediately in the region, these shocks do not stay contained. They ripple through global energy systems, affecting prices, supply, and stability, reinforcing the need to phase out fossil fuels and expand the energy transition.

In moments like these, energy becomes very immediate, determining whether people can keep the lights on, afford fuel, or cook a meal at the end of the day. We’ve seen this before. During the 2022 global energy crisis, rising fuel prices threatened to push an estimated 100 million people back toward polluting cooking fuels, reversing years of progress. In many parts of Sub-Saharan Africa and Asia, where access is already fragile, households were among the first to absorb these shocks.

Clean cooking sits within this broader reality. It’s not separate from the conversations we’re having today around energy, crisis, and uncertainty. Access to something as basic as cooking is often one of the first things to shift when conditions deteriorate.

I’ve been thinking a lot about this through conversations with colleagues at UNDP working on energy justice. How the ongoing atrocities don’t just affect one country or one region, but are part of a larger, interconnected system. From whether households can afford to cook, to how countries respond to shifting energy supplies, to what this means for the future of renewables and the critical minerals behind them.

Access to energy remains one of the most important development challenges, with more than 1 billion people still living without reliable and affordable energy.

But the challenge is no longer only scale only, it is how we navigate complexity.

Energy planning must now account for multiple interacting dimensions: resource potential, infrastructure, crises, and climate risk. Understanding how these layers align in space—and evolve over time—is critical to directing investment where it can deliver the greatest impact.

Through a collaboration between UNDP and @IBM, we are advancing AI-powered geospatial tools to support this shift. The Clean Energy Equity Index and Electricity Access Forecasting Model provide forward-looking, spatially detailed insights across more than 100 countries, enabling more precise and integrated analysis of energy access and transition pathways. Data only creates value when it is integrated into decisions and financing.

Operationalizing these data layers—embedding them into policy processes, linking them to investment pipelines, and supporting the identification of bankable, high-impact interventions—is the next step.

Green industrialization is not just about scaling renewables. It is about rebuilding one of the largest energy-consuming systems in the global economy — where industry accounts for 30% of global energy use, yet still relies on fossil fuels for more than 60% of it.

Yesterday, I participated in the "Building from the Belém Declaration on Global Green Industrialization — First Full Meeting of Supporting Countries and Organizations", organized by UNIDO  and the Brazilian government ahead of the International Vienna Energy and Climate Forum (IVECF) . With $1 trillion in industrial decarbonization projects in the pipeline but few reaching final investment decision, three opportunities stood out:

	1.	Align energy, industry, and trade strategies. Green industrialization is becoming a source of competitive advantage. The global clean energy market could grow from $1.2 trillion to $3 trillion by 2035.

	2.	Integrate digital systems and AI into decisions. AI alone could reduce energy sector emissions by 1.3–2.6 Gt CO2 annually — equivalent to the EU's total emissions today.

	3.	Coordinate infrastructure, policy, and finance. The constraint is no longer capital. With financing costs up to 7x higher in key markets, system alignment will determine where the next generation of industry is built.

Green industrialization is now a question of system design. The countries that move first to align demand, infrastructure, and finance will not only decarbonize, they will shape the next phase of industrial growth.

#GreenIndustrialization #IVECF2026 #EnergyforDevelopment

Energy systems are being reshaped in real time. 

This is not just a transition; it is reshaping the global energy economy.

Yesterday, I had the great opportunity to participate in a session hosted by the GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization)  at the  (International Vienna Energy and Climate Forum (IVECF) ) — where this convergence was at the centre of the discussion alongside GEIDCO's Chairman, Mr. Xin Baoan.

Rising geopolitical tensions and the rapid acceleration of AI and digital infrastructure are reshaping development priorities. Conflicts and instability are exposing the vulnerability of concentrated energy systems, reinforcing the need for resilience, security, and diversification of supply. At the same time, surging electricity demand — driven by AI and cooling needs set to triple by 2050 — is placing new and growing pressures on already strained energy systems.

Meanwhile, innovation is advancing rapidly. Clean energy technologies could reach $2 trillion by 2035, and nearly $5.8 trillion is expected to flow into grid upgrades between 2026 and 2035. Yet this opportunity remains unevenly distributed — with innovation, capital, and infrastructure still concentrated in too few countries.

Three actions are needed to change this:
	1.	Treat resilience as a core investment priority. Every $1 invested in resilient infrastructure yields more than $4 in benefits. Countries with stronger renewable systems are already better absorbing shocks. Structural investments in wind, solar, and stronger grids are the answer — not short-term subsidies that address symptoms, not system constraints.

	2.	Build the skills, institutions, and infrastructure to deliver at scale. Capacity building is not just training — it is about building the jobs and technical capability countries need to absorb rising investment, including $635 billion in digital infrastructure in 2026. With fewer than 5% of people in low-income countries holding basic digital skills, closing this gap is essential for the Global South to move from hosting digital infrastructure to building the energy systems that power it.

	3.	Strengthen South-South cooperation and regional interconnectivity. Initiatives such as the ASEAN Power Grid, Just Energy Transition Partnerships, and Mission 300 show how coordination can unlock larger, more resilient, and investable systems — and help developing countries capture more value from the transition.

This is the largest development opportunity of our time — and the moment to align systems to deliver it.
#IVECF2026 #EnergyTransition #GreenIndustrialization #SDG7

What if solar panels didn’t stop working when it rains—but actually produced even more energy?

Scientists in Spain have developed a new hybrid solar technology that can generate electricity from both sunlight and raindrops, opening a new path for all-weather renewable energy.

Researchers at the Institute of Materials Science of Seville (ICMS), part of the Spanish National Research Council and the University of Seville, designed a thin-film device built on advanced perovskite solar cells. This system not only captures sunlight efficiently but also harvests energy from falling raindrops.

Here’s how it works:

☀️ The perovskite layer converts sunlight into electricity, like next-generation solar panels
💧 A specially engineered surface generates electrical charge when raindrops hit it, using mechanical energy from impact and motion

In controlled lab conditions, researchers observed that a single raindrop can generate a measurable electrical output, showing the strong potential of this dual-energy system.

⚡ Why this matters:
Traditional solar panels often lose efficiency during cloudy or rainy weather. This innovation helps solve that limitation by turning rain into an additional energy source instead of a disruption.

It could be especially useful for:

Outdoor environmental sensors
Smart agriculture systems
Internet of Things (IoT) devices
Remote and off-grid installations

🌍 The bigger impact:
This technology points toward a future where renewable energy systems are more stable, adaptable, and weather-resilient. Instead of relying only on sunshine, energy systems could one day harvest power from multiple natural sources at once.

What if the real gap in digital energy innovation is not technology, but whether national innovation systems are enabling young builders in low-access settings?
 
That was at the heart of discussions today during the SDG 7 segment of the 2026 ECOSOC Youth Forum at the United Nations  Headquarters in New York, alongside A. Anastasia Kefalidou and Elsy T. Milan.
 
Young people are already driving solutions in energy access, mini-grid management, and digital service delivery. But to unlock many of these ideas require to create national innovation systems that connect policy, financing and technology innovation to scale.
 
This matters because over 85% of the world’s youth live in developing countries where energy poverty, climate vulnerability, and unemployment are most acute, and where innovation needs stronger support.
 
Three reflections stand out:

	1.	Scaling digital energy systems requires solutions that reflect local realities. Southeast Asia’s AI startups attracted over USD 2 billion, but in places like the Pacific, where around 1,500 languages are spoken, tools that ignore local context may scale technically while failing in practice.

	2.	Youth innovation delivers most when energy systems are built to absorb it. Young innovators are already responding to local needs. In Kenya, Nigeria, and Rwanda, youth-led pay-as-you-go solar platforms are already using IoT and mobile money data to manage connections and improve planning.

	3.	Digital energy tools matter only if they advance real development outcomes. More than 1.18 billion people still live in energy poverty, while the world enters a multi-trillion-dollar digital infrastructure investment cycle. The real question is whether capital, data, and innovation are reaching the places where they can have the greatest human impact.

Young people are not waiting to be included in the transition. They are already building it. The task now is to align systems around them so their solutions can deliver at scale.
 
#ECOSOCYouthForum #SDG7 #EnergyAccess #DigitalTransformation #YouthInnovation

Engineers in the UAE built floating solar panels that do two things at once — generate clean electricity and turn seawater into fresh drinking water using only the power they produce. In a region where fresh water is scarcer than oil, this changes everything.

The system developed by Khalifa University combines standard photovoltaic panels with integrated membrane distillation desalination units mounted on the same floating platform. Solar panels generate electricity from direct sunlight while the heat absorbed by panel surfaces that normally reduces electrical efficiency is captured and redirected to heat seawater for membrane distillation below the panel layer. This dual harvesting of both solar electricity and solar heat — normally wasted — gives the combined system 40% better overall energy utilization than using solar panels and desalination separately.

Each floating platform measuring 100 square meters generates 18 kilowatts of electricity and produces 20,000 liters of fresh drinking water daily using only the heat and light from the same sun. The platform's buoyant design also reduces water surface evaporation by 30% beneath it, conserving water in the reservoirs and coastal areas where platforms are deployed. UAE's pilot installation of 50 platforms off Abu Dhabi's coast already supplies fresh water to a coastal community of 12,000 residents.

The UAE plans 5,000 platforms covering 50 square kilometers of coastal water by 2027, generating 900 megawatts of electricity and 1 billion liters of fresh water daily — enough clean water for the entire Abu Dhabi emirate from ocean alone.
Source: Khalifa University Abu Dhabi, UAE Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure, 2025

I had the opportunity to engage with Federal Minister of Energy, Mining and Industry Vedran Lakic  on advancing this agenda, grounded in a clear and forward-looking vision for the Federation of BiH.

We discussed three priorities that are key to Bosnia and Herzegovina's energy transition:

1. Integrating energy modeling, data, and AI to enhance energy planning and identify investment opportunities: With significant reliance on coal for electricity and around $6 billion needed to modernize the energy system, integrating data, modeling, and AI can help plan a more secure and cost-effective energy future while guiding smarter investments.

2. Leveraging energy efficiency as a driver for economic transformation: Bosnia and Herzegovina’s economy remains significantly more energy-intensive than the EU average, requiring more energy to produce the same output. Improving efficiency across heating, services, and industry can lower costs, strengthen competitiveness, and free up capital for growth and investment.

3. Advancing a just energy transition to foster green job creation through coal phase-down policies: With 15,000–20,000 workers in the coal sector, the transition offers an opportunity to reskill and shift jobs toward renewables, efficiency, and modern grids—critical in addressing long-term brain drain and building a future-oriented workforce.

UNDP  stands ready and is pleased to support the Federal Ministry of Energy, Mining and Industry in translating this vision into concrete actions to advance a just energy transition in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

I had the opportunity to engage with Federal Minister of Energy, Mining and Industry Vedran Lakic  on advancing this agenda, grounded in a clear and forward-looking vision for the Federation of BiH.

We discussed three priorities that are key to Bosnia and Herzegovina's energy transition:

1. Integrating energy modeling, data, and AI to enhance energy planning and identify investment opportunities: With significant reliance on coal for electricity and around $6 billion needed to modernize the energy system, integrating data, modeling, and AI can help plan a more secure and cost-effective energy future while guiding smarter investments.

2. Leveraging energy efficiency as a driver for economic transformation: Bosnia and Herzegovina’s economy remains significantly more energy-intensive than the EU average, requiring more energy to produce the same output. Improving efficiency across heating, services, and industry can lower costs, strengthen competitiveness, and free up capital for growth and investment.

3. Advancing a just energy transition to foster green job creation through coal phase-down policies: With 15,000–20,000 workers in the coal sector, the transition offers an opportunity to reskill and shift jobs toward renewables, efficiency, and modern grids—critical in addressing long-term brain drain and building a future-oriented workforce.

UNDP  stands ready and is pleased to support the Federal Ministry of Energy, Mining and Industry in translating this vision into concrete actions to advance a just energy transition in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Today, I had the pleasure of engaging with United Nations  colleagues working across jobs, health, gender, and sustainable development in Bosnia and Herzegovina—areas all connected by one common thread: a just energy transition.

In today’s geopolitical context—marked by price volatility, supply risks, and shifting energy alliances—this transition becomes a clear opportunity for BiH:
•	From coal dependence to economic diversification – coal still accounts for 47% of energy supply and over $400 million in exports, but transitioning can unlock new industries and reduce exposure to external shocks 
•	From energy vulnerability to security and growth – with a target of 43.6% renewables by 2030, BiH can strengthen energy independence while creating new economic opportunities.

The transition is about transforming an existing energy system into a more competitive, resilient, and future-ready economy. How do we accelerate and align this shift?

1.	Strengthen the grid to drive growth: With over $6 billion needed and renewables rising, the priority is integration. A stronger, digital grid unlocks capacity, reliability, and competitiveness.

2.	Turn coal into a just transition pathway: Coal supports jobs and exports but also creates an entry point for reskilling and new industries. This is strategic to shift from job loss and brain drain to creating jobs and retaining talent.

3.	Make efficiency an economic strategy: With buildings using over 50% of energy, efficiency is the fastest way to cut costs, improve air quality, and strengthen resilience, especially when scaled through data and digital tools.

4.	Unlocking private investment to scale bankable energy pipelines – with over $405 million in electricity exports, BiH has a strong foundation to attract investment and position itself as a competitive clean energy supplier

UNDP, together with the wider UN system, stands ready to support Bosnia and Herzegovina in shaping and delivering this just energy transition pathway.
#JustEnergyTransition #SDG7 #EnergyForDevelopment

⚡At #EAIF2026, a high-level panel on the state of funding for private sector–driven electricity access set the stage for an important conversation on achieving #SDG7.

Panelists, including UNDP’s Mateo Salomon, Head of Climate Change Mitigation, reflected on how the landscape is shifting. The discussion highlighted that funding and technology are no longer the primary barriers—rather, the challenge lies in how risks are understood, shared, and managed across public, private, and development actors.

Key issues included persistent currency risk, which continues to deter long-term investment, as well as gaps in early-stage and project preparation financing that limit the pipeline of bankable projects. The conversation also pointed to the need to better connect investment with demand, particularly by scaling productive use of energy to strengthen project viability and long-term impact.

Mateo highlighted the Africa Minigrids Program (AMP) as an example of how these challenges can be addressed in practice. In Somalia, AMP has supported the development of an enabling environment for private sector engagement, including progress toward licensing Electricity Service Providers and establishing the country’s first national tariff framework.

The energy transition is the largest job creator of our time. Will those jobs drive development, or deepen divides?

Every major energy shift reshapes not only how societies are powered, but who gets to work, learn, and build wealth. Clean energy already employs over 76 million people worldwide. EV manufacturing alone added nearly 800,000 jobs in 2025.

But scale does not guarantee fairness. Without deliberate policy, the transition risks concentrating value in a few markets, while others remain locked into extraction and low-value assembly instead of capturing innovation and industrial growth.

So how can this become a real development accelerator for the Global South?

⚙️ Turn clean energy opportunities into national innovation ecosystems
Jobs do not come from talent alone, but from systems. Moving from fossil fuel to green-based economies requires a full ecosystem: industrial strategy for building domestic value chains, skills systems for aligning workforce capabilities, and investment frameworks for mobilizing and de-risking capital. 
When policy, finance, and  human capital are aligned, clean energy deployment translates into local value

👩‍🎓Leverage the convergence of energy, digital data, and AI to unlock new labour markets
The next wave of energy jobs will not only be in infrastructure, but in intelligence. For a global youth population of 1.8 billion, this represents a transformative opportunity :the integration of digital technologies, data systems, and AI into energy systems — from smart grids to predictive maintenance and energy planning — is creating entirely new categories of high-skilled jobs.

🌍 Make the Global South a source of innovation, not only deployment
When countries co-develop technologies, skills, and value chains, they capture far more value than by importing solutions alone. The energy transition will create millions of jobs. Whether it also creates resilient industries, inclusive livelihoods, and fair pathways for today's workforce will depend on the choices governments, investors, and institutions make now.

This week in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I am meeting partners, universities, and young people — in a country where 15,000 coal workers stand at the frontier of transition, where sites like, Zenica, Gračanica and Kreka are being repurposed from coal to solar, and where a new generation is ready to build the country's next economy.

Green jobs are how we make that possible. This is the conversation we need to have everywhere.

#JustEnergyTransition #GreenJobs #EnergyForDevelopment
Renaud Meyer Alexander De Croo  Dr. Abdallah Dardari

The air in Zenica tells a story before you even step underground.

Coal has long been at the center of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s economy,  with miners once a national symbol, even featured on the country’s currency. Now, that legacy is shifting. Across the country’s coal system, employment  is being reshaped as mines restructure and gradually close.

Today, our team at UNDP  met with the Director of RM Zenica and his team , one of the country’s most significant coal sites. Zenica is part of the coal phase-down program, helping shape how Bosnia and Herzegovina can manage a gradual transition in line with its longer-term reform and EU accession pathway.

And given that coal has been central to the country’s economy, communities, and livelihoods, three priorities stand out:
- Reskilling as a development opportunity: Across the country, around 15,000–20,000 jobs are linked to the coal sector, while over 157,000 work in manufacturing — much of it historically supported by coal. As closures accelerate, the challenge is ensuring that new employment pathways are developed, accessible, and aligned with market demand.

- Land and economic renewal: With declining productivity and rising costs, the opportunity lies in transforming former mining assets into new engines of local growth — from clean energy to green industrial redevelopment.

- Building a national innovation ecosystem to accelerate the transition:  Coordinated action across policy, finance, education systems, and the private sector is essential to translate transition plans into real investments, skills, and jobs on the ground. 

Zenica reflects a broader shift underway across coal regions, where communities are navigating complex economic and social change.
This change means ensuring that workers who fueled energy systems for generations are not left behind. 

It means delivering tangible outcomes for workers and their families — creating stable jobs, restoring economic confidence, and ensuring that communities like Zenica remain at the center of the country’s future.

Where is the next model of development actually being built?
 
Today, we are celebrating “Earth” day, while we live on a largely Ocean planet.
 
Over 40% of the world’s population lives in coastal areas. 
More than 80% of global goods move across the ocean. 
And over 99% of communications depend on submarine cables.
 
At Shanghai Climate Week 2026, on World Earth Day, I reflected on how marine and island regions are accelerating as the testing ground for the next development model.
 
Across SIDS, energy is converging with geospatial data, digital platforms, and AI.
One integrated system shaping how countries plan, invest, and grow.
 
If SIDS meet their renewable energy targets, they could unlock over 13 GW of capacity and save up to $3.3 billion annually, building resilience to energy shocks cascade across food, water, tourism, and transport.
 
The question is how to get there. Three shifts are defining this transition:
 
1. Connect energy, oceans, and economies through data
Island states manage ocean territories up to 25 times larger than their landmass. Today, geospatial tools are making this scale manageabl, such as Digital Earth Pacific which pool 30 years of satellite data to monitor over 34,000 km of coastline while reducing costs by 90%.
 
2. Redesign finance around integrated systems
SIDS need at least $11.7 billion annually for adaptation through 2035, yet receive only a small share of global climate finance. The constraint is not only capital, but structure. Capital follows clarity. It requires pipelines, credible data, and risk-informed planning. Tools like the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index are shifting access from income to vulnerability.
 
3. Build national innovation systems
The transition is not delivered project by project. It is built as a system. In the Maldives, a $50 million sovereign space fund is enabling real-time monitoring of coastal risks and infrastructure. Across island states, energy, digital, and data ecosystems are being designed together to support resilience and new industries.
 
Through initiatives like the Green and Digital Innovation Project, UNDP is working together with partners to build and scale these models starting in Baoting and beyond, integrating green and digital innovation into energy systems and developing climate-resilient models that can be shared globally.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment

In a school in Banja Luka, winter no longer means cold classrooms. Energy efficiency renovations have cut energy use by nearly half. Classrooms are warmer, costs are lower, and air quality has improved.
 
It is a simple example, but it shows what Bosnia and Herzegovina now has the opportunity to scale, turning environmental pressure into healthier cities and new economic pathways.
 
I had the opportunity to meet with the Federal Ministry of Environment and Tourism of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and with the Minister of Civil Engineering Spatial Planning and Ecology, where we discussed how environmental policy can actively shape and accelerate the energy transition.
 
Our exchange focused on three priorities.
 
First, energy efficiency as a direct path to cleaner air and economic relief. Bosnia and Herzegovina is almost four times more energy-intensive than the EU average, with buildings and heating driving a large share of emissions. This gap is an opportunity. Deep renovation can cut energy use and emissions by 30 to 50 percent while reducing costs for households and the public sector.
 
Second, air quality as a system-level priority. Air pollution is linked to over 3,000 premature deaths each year. In cities like Sarajevo and Tuzla, winter pollution can exceed WHO limits by 5 to 8 times. Data and digital tools can change this and identify solutions. Real-time monitoring and AI-based forecasting can identify hotspots, predict peaks, and enable targeted action.
 
Third, former mining areas as platforms for new growth. Thousands of hectares of degraded land can be restored and repurposed. Across Europe, similar sites are now hosting large-scale solar and new industries. For Bosnia and Herzegovina, this is a pathway to restore land, create jobs, and position former coal regions at the center of a new development model.
 
Bosnia and Herzegovina has the foundations to go further. By linking environmental policy, energy systems, and land use, the country can position itself as a regional innovation hub for just energy transition.
 
UNDP stands ready to support the Ministries in advancing these priorities, bringing in regional experience, data-driven tools, and investment support to translate environmental policy into tangible results for people and the economy.

This week, I had an insightful exchange with colleagues from the Ministery of Foreign Trade and Economic Relations, a key institution at the center of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s energy transition. 

MoFTER plays a critical bridging role, connecting national priorities with regional and global commitments, from EU accession and the Energy Community to climate obligations under the #UNFCCC. 

What stood out is the vision to position the just energy transition as a driver of broader economic and societal transformation. This is being shaped through key frameworks, including energy targets, the draft National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP), and a modern electricity law: 

The electricity law is particularly important as it sets the rules for how the power system operates, including market structure, pricing, and grid access. It is key to aligning with EU energy acquis and creating the conditions to scale renewables and attract investment.  
While the NECP sets a clear direction, moving towards implementation remains the main challenge, particularly given the need for inter-entity alignment, financing, and institutional coordination. 
With 56-60% of electricity still generated from coal and around $6 billion needed for modernization, these frameworks are essential to guide investment and reform. 

Energy is being linked to broader development goals, from attracting talent to creating jobs. This is critical in a country where industry contributes 20-25% of GDP and employs over 150,000 people, while 15,000-20,000 coal workers will need reskilling to support a just transition to green jobs. 

For UNDP , this is where partnership matters most: supporting MoFTER in turning strategy into implementation and connecting national efforts with international support and financing.
#EnergyForDevelopment

Over the past few days in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I’ve been thinking a lot about what a just energy transition really looks like in practice. 
  
Not just in policy frameworks or investment plans, but on the ground, in places like Gračanica, Gornja Breza, and Višća: sites that have powered the country for decades and now sit at the center of its next chapter. 
 
These are not just coal mines. They are local economies, identities, and livelihoods. 
  
Through engagement with Stela Melnic, Director of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development for BiH, we discussed the growing momentum to repurpose sites like these into renewable energy assets, turning former extraction zones into hubs for clean energy. 
 
At Gračanica alone, there is a plan to develop a 50 MW solar power plant on rehabilitated mining land, with an investment of nearly €40 million and supported by international financing such as EBRD. The country’s mining history is reshaping its clean energy future.  
 
More broadly, the -#EBRD is scaling renewables, upgrading grids and storage, supporting market reforms, and investing in energy efficiency and emerging technologies to accelerate decarbonization while strengthening energy security and resilience.
 
What’s clear is that financing the transition is not only about capital, but building a pipeline of bankable projects, de-risking investment, and aligning goals with implementation. 
  
And at the core of it all is one question: what does “just” mean in practice?

What if the real gap in digital energy innovation is not technology, but whether national innovation systems are enabling young builders in low-access settings?
 
That was at the heart of discussions today during the SDG 7 segment of the 2026 ECOSOC Youth Forum at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, alongside A. Anastasia Kefalidou and Elsy T. Milan .
 
Young people are already driving solutions in energy access, mini-grid management, and digital service delivery. But to unlock many of these ideas require to create national innovation systems that connect policy, financing and technology innovation to scale.
 
This matters because over 85% of the world’s youth live in developing countries where energy poverty, climate vulnerability, and unemployment are most acute, and where innovation needs stronger support.
 
Three reflections stand out:

	1.	Scaling digital energy systems requires solutions that reflect local realities. Southeast Asia’s AI startups attracted over USD 2 billion, but in places like the Pacific, where around 1,500 languages are spoken, tools that ignore local context may scale technically while failing in practice.

	2.	Youth innovation delivers most when energy systems are built to absorb it. Young innovators are already responding to local needs. In Kenya, Nigeria, and Rwanda, youth-led pay-as-you-go solar platforms are already using IoT and mobile money data to manage connections and improve planning.

	3.	Digital energy tools matter only if they advance real development outcomes. More than 1.18 billion people still live in energy poverty, while the world enters a multi-trillion-dollar digital infrastructure investment cycle. The real question is whether capital, data, and innovation are reaching the places where they can have the greatest human impact.

Young people are not waiting to be included in the transition. They are already building it. The task now is to align systems around them so their solutions can deliver at scale. #ECOSOCYouthForum #SDG7 #EnergyAccess #DigitalTransformation #YouthInnovation

To conclude his mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Riad Meddeb delivered a lecture at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering in Sarajevo, engaging with students on the role of youth in shaping a sustainable and low-carbon future.

The discussion highlighted the importance of new generations not only as the future workforce, but as active drivers of change in the green and just transition.

A little reflection: I have spent over 25 years working across development, from labor and livelihoods to energy transitions, climate, and sustainable development. I started at the UN as an intern, learning how many roadmaps exist within the system, all aiming toward one goal: creating real impact for people and communities. 

Why am I sharing this? Because when I began my career, my generation aimed to create an impact for communities on the ground. As my work expands, it is often the moments with the next generation of leaders that remind me why I chose this path in the first place. 

To close out a great week of consultations across Bosnia and Herzegovina, I met with students at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering and Economics in the University of Sarajevo to discuss something central to the country’s future: the link between energy, digitalization, and opportunity. 

For Bosnia and Herzegovina, the opportunity is real. More than 2,000 MW of new renewable capacity is planned by 2030, yet youth outmigration remains one of the biggest risks. Around 270,000 young people are considering leaving, nearly half of the youth surveyed. Amid these realities, the green economy is creating entirely new demand for engineers, innovators, and problem-solvers.

We spoke about how the clean energy transition is no longer only about producing power, but about designing systems around constraints: smarter grids, storage, AI-driven planning, and local industries that create value and jobs. And as engineers themselves, they are entering the workforce at a moment where they can help define the systems that will shape it. 

Because the future of the transition will depend on whether young people see that they can build that future here.

Where is the next model of development actually being built?
 
Today, we are celebrating “Earth” day, while we live on a largely Ocean planet.
 
Over 40% of the world’s population lives in coastal areas. 
More than 80% of global goods move across the ocean. 
And over 99% of communications depend on submarine cables.
 
At Shanghai Climate Week 2026, on World Earth Day, I reflected on how marine and island regions are accelerating as the testing ground for the next development model.
 
Across SIDS, energy is converging with geospatial data, digital platforms, and AI.
One integrated system shaping how countries plan, invest, and grow.
 
If SIDS meet their renewable energy targets, they could unlock over 13 GW of capacity and save up to $3.3 billion annually, building resilience to energy shocks cascade across food, water, tourism, and transport.
 
The question is how to get there. Three shifts are defining this transition:
 
1. Connect energy, oceans, and economies through data
Island states manage ocean territories up to 25 times larger than their landmass. Today, geospatial tools are making this scale manageabl, such as Digital Earth Pacific which pool 30 years of satellite data to monitor over 34,000 km of coastline while reducing costs by 90%.
 
2. Redesign finance around integrated systems
SIDS need at least $11.7 billion annually for adaptation through 2035, yet receive only a small share of global climate finance. The constraint is not only capital, but structure. Capital follows clarity. It requires pipelines, credible data, and risk-informed planning. Tools like the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index are shifting access from income to vulnerability.
 
3. Build national innovation systems
The transition is not delivered project by project. It is built as a system. In the Maldives, a $50 million sovereign space fund is enabling real-time monitoring of coastal risks and infrastructure. Across island states, energy, digital, and data ecosystems are being designed together to support resilience and new industries.
 
Through initiatives like the Green and Digital Innovation Project, UNDP is working together with partners to build and scale these models starting in Baoting and beyond, integrating green and digital innovation into energy systems and developing climate-resilient models that can be shared globally. #EnergyForDevelopment

What if the future of energy systems is being built across the ocean, coastlines and islands?

Across Small Island Developing States 🏝️, a different model is taking shape. One where energy is not only about power, but about integrating water, food systems, ecosystems, climate resilience, and innovation.

This is why we increasingly see SIDS not just as small states, but as large ocean states and digital islands, where the energy transition becomes a platform for broader economic transformation.

With many SIDS importing up to 90% of their fuel, the transition to renewables is not only about decarbonization, it is about reducing exposure, creating fiscal space, and strengthening economic resilience. If national renewable energy targets are achieved, #SIDS could save up to USD 3.3 billion annually, equivalent to roughly 3.3% of regional GDP.

Therefore, the answer is not within the energy sector itself, but in how energy connects across systems – food, fisheries, tourism, mobility, health, and local enterprise.

With less than 1% of land typically suitable for agriculture, many islands rely heavily on imports. This is driving innovation in localized production systems, including vertical and urban agriculture models.

Tourism drives 10–70% of GDP in many Pacific island economies, yet a significant share of that value is lost to fuel imports. Hotels, transport, and services are often powered by diesel costing $1–2 per litre, meaning that part of every tourist dollar quickly leaves the economy.

Integrating to renewables with the integration of digital, data and AI solutions, change that equation, reducing operating costs and allowing more of that value to be retained and reinvested locally. Clean energy systems are already reshaping how islands produce food, move people and goods, manage water, and protect marine ecosystems, from agriculture and fisheries to e-mobility and port infrastructure.

What is emerging is a new model, where systems are becoming more resilient, more intelligent, and more connected to real economies.

Rising Up for SIDS means recognizing islands not as the frontline of vulnerability, but as innovation hubs for global resilience.

#RisingUpforSIDS #EnergyforDevelopment
Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS) Alexander De Croo

Last week, the International Energy Agency (IEA) released its flagship report on energy technologies, the Energy Technology Perspectives. It is typically rich, spanning technology deployment and manufacturing, as well as project pipelines, investments, and trade. Some interesting findings:

1) The combined global market value for clean energy technologies has grown 20% on average per year over the past decade, to reach nearly USD 1.2 trillion in 2025. Without accounting for increased ambition, this could reach USD 2 trillion by 2035 (the same size as the global crude oil market in 2025). If the policies countries say they will implement are accounted for, this market grows to USD 3 trillion over the next decade;

2) The growth of this market will have profound implications for trade. Under Stated Policies, the global value of net trade in clean energy technologies more than doubles over the next decade, from USD 290 billion in 2025, to USD 620 billion by 2035;

3) There are clear winners here. By 2035, China’s clean technology exports are effectively equal in value to their oil imports (see charts below)

4) EVs are a big part of this China clean energy technology story, and the protagonists here are shifting fast. Emerging economies accounted for less than 5% of China’s EV exports in 2020, but now represent nearly 40%. 

5) How has it sped so far ahead? Accumulated advantages across innovation; largescale production; manufacturing efficiency; a skilled workforce; integrated supply chains and access to cheap resources and labour. All reinforced by consistent policy and financial support.

6) The EU-China cost gap is explained by different factors across different technologies. For batteries, higher manufacturing efficiency accounts for over 40% of the cost difference. Energy and labour cost differences account for a large share of the cost gap with Europe in energy and labour-intensive steps, such as upstream solar PV manufacturing (65% of the gap) and in wind blade production (75%). 

7) So what can countries do to compete? They identify and play to their strengths and look to strategic partnerships. For example, producing solar PV modules made in the European Union with imported wafers from North Africa, where energy input costs are comparatively low, could cost almost 20% less than producing a fully EU-made module.

Congratulations to Timur Gül, Araceli Fernandez Pales , Peter Levi and the ETP team for producing this excellent report, which you can read here: https://lnkd.in/ef7Wt-kc

The lack of access to clean cooking costs Africa USD 791 billion every year in health, economic, and environmental losses. This is equivalent to around one fifth of the continent’s GDP.
 
I was pleased to contribute to the Africa Regional Forum on Sustainable Development 12, where we discussed how accelerating clean cooking can unlock broader development outcomes.
 
Clean cooking is one of the highest-return investments available today. The question is no longer whether we can afford it, but whether we can afford not to.
 
What is changing now is how the sector is being transformed through three structural shifts:
 
First, data and digital tools to scale solutions.
Geospatial tools, AI, and digital platforms are helping map demand, monitor usage, and align supply with real needs. In Rwanda, where access stood at just 8 percent in 2022, a data-driven pathway now projects over 3.4 million households adopting clean cooking solutions by 2029.
 
Second, building markets at scale.
Sub-Saharan Africa needs around USD 4 billion annually by 2030, yet investment remains far below this. Clean cooking must be treated as an economy to build, with investable pipelines that unlock public and private finance.
 
Third, integrating clean cooking into energy planning.
In Kenya and Uganda, e-cooking tariffs are making electric cooking more affordable by aligning policy with real household demand. This is the direction of the UNDP–AFREC Beyond Stoves initiative, advancing policy reform, gender-responsive institutions, and market development.
 
With Mission 300 gaining momentum, the Clean Cooking Summit in Kenya and the SDG7 review at the High-Level Political Forum in 2026 will be a window of opportunity for the clean cooking agenda.
 
Through #UN-Energy, which brings together more than 30 UN entities, we have a platform to align efforts, strengthen coherence, and accelerate delivery across the system.
 
UNDP  stands ready to support countries in moving from ambition to implementation, so that clean cooking becomes a financed, gender-responsive, and coordinated pillar of Africa’s development pathway.
 
#ARFSD2026 #CleanCooking #SDG7 #EnergyforDevelopment

Two weeks ago, I had the opportunity to join a technical mission in El Salvador, supporting ongoing efforts to modernize public transport in the Área Metropolitana de San Salvador.

During the mission, we engaged at the technical level with IFIs and development partners including the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), CAF – Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, and the European Union. We also had the opportunity to interact with officials from the Ministry of Public Works and Transport, the General Directorate of Energy, Hydrocarbons and Mines, as well as other key stakeholders involved in the sector.

Building on the work highlighted below, one key takeaway stands out: transforming urban mobility is not only a technical challenge — it is also financial, regulatory, and institutional, requiring strong technical assistance closely linked to investments.

In a public transport system with numerous operators, scaling investment will require strengthened coordination, improved access to finance, risk-sharing mechanisms, innovative financial instruments (such as leasing, securitization, and blended finance), as well as robust regulatory and governance frameworks.

There is a significant opportunity to support the development of a more integrated, efficient, and low-emission public transport system. In this context, United Nations Development Programme can support strategic technical assistance associated with innovative financial instruments, as well as policy and financial de-risking, to help scale up investments and maximize development impact.

What frontiers are #SIDS 🏝️ leading in when it comes to sustainable energy innovation?
 
Is it about
🌱 Vertical and urban farming, where food production depends on energy in places with less than 1% arable land
🏝️ Tourism economies generating 20 to 70% of GDP, yet losing value through diesel at 1 to 2 dollars per litre
🚤 E-mobility and marine transport reshaping connectivity, trade, and fisheries
🏙️ Digital islands, with urban centers growing around 4% annually as new economic hubs
🌊 Coastal adaptation, where erosion, flooding, and infrastructure risks require energy and spatial planning together
 
At the Pacific SIDS Regional Energy Symposium in Port Moresby, I reflected on how sustainable energy is not only driving an energy transition, but shaping a new model for development in SIDS.
 
What is emerging across SIDS:
 
1. Geospatial and AI-driven planning: With platforms like Digital Earth Pacific mapping over 34,000 kilometers of coastline, countries can identify risks and prioritize investments with far greater precision. Through the SIDS Data Platform, UNDP supports this with more than 4,000 indicators and 80 geospatial datasets.
 
2. Energy-linked whole island value chains: In Tonga, solar-powered mini-factories produce around 260,000 litres of coconut products annually. In Samoa, clean energy is extending into transport and fisheries, supported by low-carbon marine engines and more than 80 EV charging stations.
 
3. Financing distributed energy at scale: Under UNDP’s Pacific Green Transformation Project, supported by the Government of Japan, a 1 megawatt solar farm in Buin is reducing electricity costs by up to 50%, strengthening energy security, and benefiting more than 30,000 people.
 
UNDP, working across the Pacific, Caribbean, and AIS regions, is supporting this transformation through the “Rising Up for SIDS” Energy Offer, developed with AOSIS and rapidly operationalized following the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda.

With the 6th Pacific Regional Energy and Transport Ministers’ Meeting next week and pre-COP preparations ahead of #COP31, the task is clear: scale progress faster with the partnerships, finance, and tools to match SIDS’ ambition.

If you are working in this space, please reach out to us. As UNDP , we are ready to partner and support.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #RisingUpForSIDS

Can Africa turn SDG 7 ⚡️progress into Agenda 2063 transformation fast enough to leave no one behind?
 
Electrification across Africa rose from 51 percent in 2017 to 61 percent in 2023, giving more than 120 million people access to electricity, with Northern Africa near universal access and strong gains in Eastern and Western Africa.
 
Yet the gaps remain stark: more than 560 million Africans still lack electricity, and over 940 million lack clean cooking. In many communities, energy poverty is still felt as household smoke, fuel collection time and health burdens borne mainly by women.
 
I was pleased to contribute to the Affordable and Clean Energy session at the Twelfth Africa Regional Forum on Sustainable Development in Addis Ababa, where we discussed the opportunities on how SDG 7 can accelerate the 2030 Agenda and Agenda 2063.
 
The question is no longer whether Africa has ambition. It does. The question is how we move from targets to investment, delivery and transformative impact.
 
Three shifts are critical.
 
⭐️First, sustainable energy must become an industrialisation agenda. Africa has about 60 percent of the world’s best solar resources, but only a small share of installed solar capacity. Algeria’s 15 GW solar target by 2035 and Morocco’s Noor Ouarzazate solar complex show what is possible.
 
⭐️Second, clean cooking must move to the centre of energy planning. Kenya’s clean cooking strategy and electric cooking pilots in Mozambique and Sierra Leone show how it can be linked to electrification, tariff reform and national power systems.
 
⭐️Third, leverage data and digital intelligence to make delivery visible and measurable. Ethiopia’s satellite-integrated electrification planning and Mozambique’s use of electrification and socio-economic data show how better targeting can support mini-grids and e-cooking.
 
UNDP  continues to support countries with geospatial tools and energy planning models, including the Clean Energy Equity Index, so policies are tracked against delivery and investors have clearer signals.
 
If countries get their decisions right, SDG 7 and Agenda 2063 can become one delivery agenda for smarter planning, stronger institutions, better investment and impact at scale.

🏛️ Governance: how we shape the skills, expertise, processes, institutions, and organisational cultures – within and beyond government – to truly engage with the potential that digital offers for energy.

I am happy to share a UNDP Lebanon, UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub (SEH), and UNDP Regional Bureau for Arab States (RBAS) publication co-authored by Riad Meddeb, Vahakn Kabakian and myself (with special thanks to Benjamin Keller, Nazim Mammadov, Fungai Matura, Aleksandra Prodan, Mohamed Bayoumi, Karim Osseiran, Mazen Awada, Husam Tubail, Naïm Darghouth and Joumana Samaha) on compensating mechanisms for distributed generation (DG) in the Arab world. 

The report argues that DG, particularly solar photovoltaic (PV) systems enabled through net metering (NM) and net billing (NB), is a critical, fast-deployable solution for Arab States to meet rapidly growing electricity demand, improve energy security, and deliver strong socio‑economic benefits, including job creation and gender empowerment. While DG has expanded in the Arab region, effective NM/NB frameworks remain limited - only 9 of 22 Arab States have them in place largely due to weak grid infrastructure, institutional constraints, and electricity subsidies that distort price signals. Drawing on global evidence and the evolution of NM in the United States, the report argues that NM can be effective for early-stage DG uptake, but countries with higher penetration could transition toward NB and compensation based on the ‘Value of Solar’ or broader ‘Distributed Energy Resource’ (DER) value frameworks to address system performance, equity, and utility financial sustainability. The report emphasizes that DG 'value' increases substantially when paired with storage and supported by digitization and AI, but stresses that success depends on grid modernization, subsidy reform, robust cost‑benefit and equity analysis, improved data collection and transparency, and clear regulatory design. 

At a time of geo-political impacts on energy markets, positioning DG as a core power‑system asset rather than marginal add‑ons can bring significant benefits to people and economies.

Yesterday, at the Pacific Regional Energy and Transport Ministers Meeting in Port Moresby, UNDP had the privilege of hosting a side event on scaling off-grid energy in the Pacific 🌿🔋.

The vibrant dialogue, moderated by our UNDP Resident Representative, Mr. Nicholas Booth, featured an exceptional panel of regional experts:

💠 Mr. Edmond Nagombi (National Energy Authority, PNG)
💠Mr. Matthew Tasale (Department of Energy, Vanuatu)

A key message echoed across the discussion: implementing enabling regulatory frameworks is crucial for accelerating the adoption of off-grid energy solutions in the Pacific. These frameworks are essential for unlocking investment, speeding up project delivery, and ensuring that infrastructure is safe, reliable, and sustainable for the communities it serves 🔧📈.

Equally important is strengthening local-level capacity to build, manage, and maintain these off-grid energy systems. The task ahead is to use that moment to scale what is already working with the partnerships, finance, technology, and capacity needed to match SIDS ambition with implementation.”

Across the Pacific, a different model of energy transition is rising 🌊
 
Not just a shift from diesel to renewables, but a whole-of-society transformation linking energy with mobility, food systems, digital infrastructure, and climate resilience.
 
In tourism-driven economies such as Fiji, Palau, Samoa, and Vanuatu, contributing 10% to 40% of GDP, renewable energy is already reducing operating costs and helping retain more value locally.
 
In French Polynesia, seawater air conditioning systems are cutting cooling electricity demand by up to 90%, showing how sustainable energy solutions can work with natural systems while improving efficiency.
 
At the 6th Pacific Regional Energy and Transport Ministers’ Meeting (PRETMM) in Port Moresby, I reflected on how this model is taking shape, not as a future vision, but as a system being built in real time.
 
🔹 Turning energy into a foundation for value chains: Electrification has increased from around 64% in 2009 to over 85% in 2022. The next frontier is what that energy enables. In Samoa, clean energy is expanding beyond electric vehicles to low-carbon outboard motors for fishing and sea transport, linking energy to livelihoods, markets, and mobility.
 
🔹 Building digital, data, and AI foundations: Energy systems need to be designed for both demand and risk. At UNDP, the SIDS Data Platform integrates over 4,000 indicators and 80+ geospatial datasets to support investment-ready, AI-enabled planning. In Tonga, a cable disruption in 2024 affected around one-third of the population for more than two weeks, highlighting the need for resilient, energy-backed digital systems. 
 
🔹 Shifting to distributed, resilient architectures: With urban centers growing at around 4% annually and geography limiting grid expansion, distributed systems are becoming central. In Papua New Guinea, where access remains around 20%, a 1 MW solar system in Bougainville is already delivering power to over 30,000 people, reducing costs by up to 50%. The new Off-Grid Regulation is now enabling these solutions to scale.
 
As the Pacific prepares to host pre-COP discussions ahead of COP31, there is a clear opportunity to bring this model to the global stage. 
 
Through Rising Up for SIDS and the SIDS Energy Offer, UNDP is working with partners to connect policy, finance, technology, and capacity into integrated systems that can scale.
 
If you are working in this space, we invite you to connect. We are ready to listen, partner, and support.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #RisingUpForSIDS

Who are new AI systems really being built for?

The global expansion of AI infrastructure is happening at extraordinary speed, but it is also opening a rare opportunity to rethink how energy, digital infrastructure, and development systems evolve together.

Right now, the world is adding roughly 255 GWh of new electricity demand every single day from the growth trajectory of AI and data centres, equivalent to connecting another medium-sized city to the grid daily.

At the 11th United Nations Forum on Science, Technology and Innovation during the side event co-organized with GEIDCO, I reflected on why this moment represents far more than a technological shift. It is increasingly becoming a restructuring of infrastructure, industrial systems, and energy demand itself.

Three opportunities stand out:

🔹 Turning AI demand into clean energy investment. In South Africa, solar wheeling models are already linking large-scale renewable generation to industrial and digital users through the national grid.

🔹 Turning energy systems into intelligent systems. In Brazil, AI-enabled monitoring is reducing transmission fault response times from hours to seconds across infrastructure carrying most of the country’s electricity.

🔹 Turning AI infrastructure into local capability and green industrial growth. Malaysia, for example, is positioning itself as a regional digital hub while linking digital expansion to broader industrial strategy.

The direction of this transition is not fixed. 

AI revolution could help countries accelerate cleaner infrastructure, strengthen sovereignty, and capture far greater value from the next wave of industrial transformation.

The difference will come down to how swiftly countries can turn this technological expansion into lasting economic and development opportunity.

#EnergyforDevelopment

Can the rapid expansion of AI and data centres become a driver of a just energy transition?

By 2030, electricity demand from data centres worldwide is projected to more than double to around 945 TWh, slightly more than Japan's entire annual electricity consumption. By 2027, AI alone could consume 4 to 6 billion cubic metres of water each year, equivalent to the annual water consumption of a country like Denmark.

Behind every AI model sits physical infrastructure, and the decisions made today on energy, grids, water, and data centres will either deepen inequality and infrastructure pressures or unlock investment, modernize systems, and expand development opportunities across the Global South. 
 
Three takeaways:

🔹 AI data centres must be embedded in national systems of innovation, not treated as isolated infrastructure. When digital and energy systems scale together, they build national innovation ecosystems. Without that integration, data centres risk serving external platforms while local capabilities remain underdeveloped.

🔹 AI infrastructure must strengthen resilience, not compete with it. In water-stressed and capacity-constrained settings, unmanaged AI growth can privilege data centres over households, health services, and small businesses, deepening inequality.

🔹 AI is becoming one of the largest new buyers of energy, and that buying power can shape entire energy systems. Without deliberate policy, grids risk being built to serve data centres at the expense of households, small businesses, and essential services. With the right frameworks, that same demand can accelerate renewable energy deployment and strengthen broader energy access.

The future of AI will depend not only on algorithms, but on how countries build the energy systems that power them.

#EnergyForDevelopment #AI #DataCenter #JustEnergyTransition

What does a just energy transition really look like in practice in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

In a school in Banja Luka, energy efficiency renovations have cut energy use by nearly half — making classrooms warmer, brighter, and easier to maintain for more than a thousand students and staff. Small changes like these signal a deeper transformation underway across the country.

In a new op-ed, "A Shared Just Energy Transition," I share why this transition is not only an energy shift, but one of the largest shared development opportunities for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Three priorities stand out:
🔹 Strengthen governance to unlock finance in renewables. Bosnia and Herzegovina's transition will require over $6 billion in investment, with the grid at the centre. With the Electricity Law and the National Energy and Climate Plan in their final stage of approval, the foundations are in place to mobilize bankable pipelines and innovative financing.

🔹 Transform coal regions into jobs, skills, and growth. Coal still employs 15,000 to 20,000 people directly and supports more than 150,000 jobs across related sectors. Repurposing mine land in Zenica, Banovići, and Kreka — with around 27 MWp of solar capacity planned — shows how existing infrastructure can be turned into productive economic assets when connected to a national innovation ecosystem.

🔹 Harness data, AI, and digital innovation to scale energy efficiency. Public buildings retrofitted through UNDP's Green Economic Development programme have already reduced energy use by 30 to 50 percent. With smart meter deployment already exceeding the 80% national target, accelerating their full use can unlock real-time data, dynamic tariffs, and stronger system resilience.

As UNDP , we stand ready to support this whole-of-system transformation by helping connect policy, finance, and technology to build resilience, create jobs, improve quality of life, and position Bosnia and Herzegovina at the forefront of the next generation of energy innovation.

🔗 More on UNDP's work in Bosnia and Herzegovina: https://lnkd.in/eSxRHd5B

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition

Sustainable and inclusive energy access is a literal catalyst to all 1️⃣7️⃣ SDGs. But how can we make it happen? We're proposing a holistic and systems-level approach to leveraging tech to drive a just energy transition. We call it the 'Digital Energy Stack' ⬇️

The ‘digital energy stack’ is 7️⃣ tech (and non-tech) components that countries need to engage with to maximise the benefits of the AI, digital, and energy revolutions. 

📊 Data: the fuel of the energy revolution. From the Big Data generated by smart meters to the ‘Thick’ Data that needs to inform service design and policymaking.

📱 Connectivity: the wired and wireless infrastructure that lets data flow between energy solutions and stakeholders – and drives energy business models. 

🌐 Compute: the ‘currency’ of the 21st century - creating opportunities for improved energy planning and delivery, but also challenges of energy and resource use.

🛣️ Digital Public Infrastructure: the ‘roads and railways’ of our digital economies and societies, DPI could deepen the impact of digital energy solutions. 

🔒 Cybersecurity: energy is critical national infrastructure. It needs to be ‘resilient-by-design’ and we need energy professionals with cyber skills.

🤖 AI: already having an impact - whether in improving energy planning or driving new approaches for credit-scoring that make energy services more accessible.

🏛️ Governance: how we shape the skills, expertise, processes, institutions, and organisational cultures – within and beyond government – to truly engage with the potential that digital offers for energy.
